extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public opinion, journalists, and public-relations professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for producing mass-appeal public messages (news, propaganda, fiction, film, PR) that gain attention, create identification, and move audiences to feel or act. Emphasizes imagery, stereotypes, suspense, and the psychology of differing 'selves' in audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid visual imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures have always been the surest way of conveying an idea, and next in order, words that call up pictures in memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Messages should be translatable into concrete pictures or phrases that evoke clear mental images. The author contrasts 'visualizers' (who think cinematically) with those having purely intuitive perception, concluding that ideas are not lucid for practical decision until they have 'visual or tactile value.' For distant or abstract events, translate them into pictures so they register beyond vague sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear handles for identification (empathy)
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular representation the handles for identification are almost always marked. You know who the hero is at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience identification (empathy) is crucial: mark characters, roles, or angles so people can identify quickly with some aspect of the picture. Subtle empathy exists, but mass appeal relies on recognizable cues that let people 'become a character' and reenact the story in their own feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the audience something to do—engage them
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must have something to do, and the contemplation of the true, the good and the beautiful is not something to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive presentation of abstract truths will not sustain broad attention. Messages should invite active mental involvement—taking sides, suspense, rooting for a victory—so the audience is exercised rather than inert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activate powerful, near-universal motifs (sex and fighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two forms of exercise which far transcend all others... They are sexual passion and fighting, and the two have so many associations with each other... a fight about sex outranks every other theme in the breadth of its appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To arouse easy and eager attention, employ motifs linked to deep passions—romance/sexuality and conflict/struggle. These motifs bridge cultural and class differences and reliably engage wide audiences; they are common handles in moving pictures, novels, and magazine fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use suspense and unfolding struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense... constitutes the difference between the masterpieces in the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the pictures at the Rivoli or the Rialto Theatres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unfolding events and the element of struggle create suspense that holds attention longer than static beauty. Even if two works are equal in 'beauty,' motion/presentation that depicts an outcome the audience is waiting for will engage far more people and for a longer time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance realism and romanticism (realistic beginning, desirable ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our popular taste is to have the drama originate in a setting realistic enough to make identification plausible and to have it terminate in a setting romantic enough to be desirable, but not so romantic as to be inconceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pure fantasy (no familiar foothold) and relentless realism (audience dislikes defeat). Begin with plausible, recognizable detail to enable identification, then move toward a romanticized/hoped-for resolution that satisfies audience desires without breaking plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform to current stereotypes for mass appeal (or pay the price)
rubrics_metrics.description: The men who make moving pictures... must adhere to the stereotypes that they find, or pay the price of frustrating expectation. The stereotypes can be altered, but not in time to guarantee success when the film is released six months from now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass communications often depend on existing stereotypes acquired from earlier experience; changing them is possible but risky and often incompatible with commercial/time constraints. Innovators can change stereotypes but face commercial resistance from managers protecting investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow the audience to take sides and supply a triumph/resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: We have to take sides. We have to be able to take sides. In the recesses of our being we must step out of the audience on to the stage, and wrestle as the hero for the victory of good over evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective narratives create clear stakes and moral alignment so audiences can emotionally commit to one side and imagine triumph or vindication. The public prefers narratives that let them climb aboard and 'ride' away from daily drudgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with plausible reality, then enlist hope (propagandist formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilful propagandist knows that while you must start with a plausible analysis, you must not keep on analyzing... the propagandist exhausts the interest in reality by a tolerably plausible beginning, and then stokes up energy for a long voyage by brandishing a passport to heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For persuasive political or ideological messages: anchor in a recognizable problem or 'real evil,' avoid tedious continued analysis, and mobilize energy by projecting an attractive future or solution. This formula works especially when private urgency meshes with public fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify which 'self' or identity you are addressing
rubrics_metrics.description: It makes a whole lot of difference whether you conceive the demand as a desire to grow fruit or to marry the white man's daughter... the self which takes charge of the instincts when we are thinking about lemons or distant acres is very different from the self which appears when we are thinking... as the outraged head of a family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People possess multiple selves (roles, identities) that are activated in different contexts; effective messaging must target the particular self likely to respond (economic self, family/honor self, patriotic self, etc.). This changes tone, framing, and which appeals (material, moral, emotional) will work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceive and shape self-interest (do not assume deterministic mappings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self and interest are both conceived somehow... men's ideas of all things and of themselves are not instinctive. They are acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume economic position automatically yields a specific opinion. Public persuasion often requires constructing or clarifying how an audience should conceive its interest; messages should present a coherent conception of interest rather than relying solely on inferred material alignment.
